title: From Tokenizer Bias to Backbone Capability: A Controlled Study of LLMs for Time Series Forecasting

problem.claim: The study investigates the effectiveness and inherent predictive capability of pre-trained LLM backbones for time series forecasting.

gap.claim: Small-dataset training and evaluation can cause Tokenizer–Detokenizer components to overfit and mask the LLM backbone's intrinsic predictive capability, leaving its actual effectiveness under debate.

contributions.claim: Designs three models with identical architectures but distinct pre-training strategies to investigate the inherent potential of LLMs for time series forecasting.
Uses large-scale pre-training to produce more unbiased Tokenizer–Detokenizer pairs integrated with the LLM backbone.
Evaluates zero-shot and few-shot forecasting performance through controlled experiments to assess the LLM backbone's capabilities.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that the LLM backbone shows some promise, but its performance remains limited and does not consistently surpass models specifically trained on large-scale time series data.
The authors report that source code is publicly available in the LLM4TS repository.

narrative_sequence.summary: LLM backbones have attracted growing interest for time series prediction.
Typical approaches patch time series, tokenize the patches for an LLM, process them with a frozen or fine-tuned backbone, and detokenize the outputs into numerical forecasts.
The effectiveness of LLMs for time series forecasting remains under debate because Tokenizer–Detokenizer components may overfit small datasets and obscure backbone capability.
The study compares three architecturally identical models with different pre-training strategies and uses large-scale pre-training to obtain more unbiased Tokenizer–Detokenizer pairs.
Controlled zero-shot and few-shot experiments suggest that the LLM backbone has some promise but remains limited relative to specialized large-scale time series models.

source_observation.claim: Tokenizer–Detokenizer components trained and evaluated on small datasets often overfit the specific data distribution and can mask backbone capability.

interpretation.claim: Input-output adaptation components can become the dominant source of apparent performance in transfer-learning pipelines.

application.claim: Use controlled pre-training strategies and larger-scale data to reduce adapter-induced bias when evaluating a pretrained backbone.

exception.claim: The reported finding concerns this abstract's time series forecasting setting and does not establish that the same bias occurs in all transfer-learning pipelines.

source_observation.claim: The LLM backbone does not consistently outperform models specifically trained on large-scale time series data.

interpretation.claim: General pretrained backbones may offer limited benefits when domain-specific models have substantial large-scale training.

application.claim: Benchmark general-purpose backbones against strong domain-specific models under controlled zero-shot and few-shot conditions.

exception.claim: The abstract reports promise and limited performance but does not establish a universal disadvantage for LLM backbones.

unknowns: Datasets, baselines, metrics, and quantitative results are not specified.
The three model architectures and pre-training strategies are not described in detail.
The effects of frozen versus fine-tuned backbones are not reported.
No independent verification of the author-reported findings is available.
